newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU mulls action to fight international bribery.
newsitem.headline: EU mulls action to fight international bribery.

text.p: The European Commission is considering legislation to force member states to fight international bribery, an area where the EU lags far behind the United States.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said on Wednesday the Commission could use provisions in the EU treaty barring national legislation or administrative practices that distort fair trade and competition.

The remarks, made at a conference on corruption in international business transactions, referred to the still widespread practice in the EU of tolerating bribes by companies to foreign officials to win international contracts.
"The possible use of (the EU treaty provision) is being considered by the Commission," Van Miert said.
He also complained about some countries which allow firms to deduct bribes from corporate tax, but did not name them.

Despite recent efforts to combat corruption in the EU, bribery to win contracts in other countries is still common, especially with large infrastucture and supply tenders. But its hidden nature makes it difficult to measure.
A recent Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) meeting on the issue said the most extensive analysis had been done by the United States.

The U.S. government found that over the past two years some 100 business deals worth $45 billion had allegedly been lost by U.S. companies because of bribery, the OECD's secretary-general Donald Johnston told the meeting.
Although EU governments condemn corruption involving their own officials, at least in principle, some often turn a blind eye when the same practices are used in the hunt for foreign contracts.
In Belgium, for example, corruption in international contracts is not only tolerated, but encouraged by tax breaks.

"Although reprehensible, secret commissions are unfortunately necessary in trade or industrial relations with other countries," Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt said in July in reply to a written question by a Belgian senator.
This contrasts with strict legislation in the United States where the threat of prosecution is a strong deterrent.
"I think the (Foreign Corrupt Practices Act) has been rather effective in the United States," Van Miert said.
The treaty provision cited by Van Miert, Article 101, allows the Commission to initiate legislation to promote free competition, but EU ministers would make the final decision.
Van Miert said it could also be used if needed to persuade EU states to implement a recent protocol aimed at fighting bribery of EU officials to obtain contracts or funds.
